vocabulary.definition: a collective name for the original peoples of North America and their descendants; also Aboriginals
the feeling of being cut off or isolated from other people, groups, or regions
to bring someone into a group in a way that minimizes or eliminates the differences between the individual and the group
independent of the laws of another state or government; self-governing
the policy of recognizing two official languages in Canada - French and English
acting in a way that breaks the laws or rules governing a society

The uniting in 1867 of present day Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia into one country, Canada. The other provinces joined later, between 1870 and 1949. The Yukon and Northwest Territories were added during this time as well.
the belief that Canada has two founding nations, Britain and France
This idea promoted the idea that Quebec was unique because of its cultural aspects (language, civil law) and should be given concessions because of it.
to fix firmly or securely
a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and a number of political units
a person given a position of nominal leadership but having no actual authority
(or colonialism) the purpose or process of a dominant country extending its control over another, weaker country or territory
a permanent characteristic of something that will always be associated with it

The doctrine that all members of the global community accept collective responsibility for the challenges that face the world and that the motives of nations and nation-states must be respected in the search for solutions. Some may see it as placing global concerns before a country's own national interests, or the best way to protect national interests.
to work with both parties in conflict to find an agreement acceptable to both
in Canada, a government policy where diverse cultures are encouraged to keep their cultural backgrounds while living together in one society
the feelings people have in identifying with their nation
the point of view that is shaped by one's background and experiences
Pluralism means that different peoples, cultures, identities, and perspectives can coexist within the same political community.
a resident of the province of Quebec

During the Quiet Revolution of the 1960s in Québec, French-Canadians saw themselves as a minority within Canada and second-class citizens within their own province, which had been French-speaking for over three hundred years but was controlled by English-speaking businesses. French Quebeckers wanted to regain control of their own province. To get such control, Quebeckers felt that Québec must be treated differently from other provinces. That is, it must be given special status (or position) within Canada to preserve French culture and to ensure that French-Canadians were given fair treatment within Canada.
a direct vote by all eligible voters on a question or issue
to restore or return to the country of birth, citizenship, or origin
a government that is responsible or accountable to the people that elects it
political independence; able to govern oneself independent of outside influences
freedom of a nation from control by any other nation
the concept that Quebec would become a sovereign, independent country while still having an economic association with Canada
a group of people wishing to achieve freedom from control by any other nation
the existing condition or state of affairs
